statement: In 26 people seen in person by medical toxicologists at 50 US sites after taking loperamide, an anti-diarrhoea medicine that is an opioid (registry cases from 2010 or 2011 to 2016; intent known for 18: 12 misuse, 6 of whom had taken it to avoid opioid withdrawal, 3 attempted self-harm and 3 young children), the registry describes frequent heart-rhythm problems: a prolonged QTc interval in 10 (38.5%), ventricular dysrhythmias in 6 or 7 (the abstract and the results differ), a widened QRS in 6 (23.1%) and a heart attack in 1, as well as coma or depressed consciousness in 11 (42.3%) and slowed breathing in 5. Seventeen needed specific treatment, 4 a breathing tube, 2 a pacemaker and 1 resuscitation; none died. Everyone with a ventricular dysrhythmia whose amount was recorded had taken far more than the label allows. These are only the cases that reached a toxicologist, the amount was known for 9 of 26 and there is no comparison group, so the series cannot show how often this happens, whether any amount is safe, or that loperamide alone caused each problem. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Doctors who treat poisonings in the USA described 26 people who became ill after taking loperamide, some of them to get through opioid withdrawal: many had dangerous changes in heart rhythm, some needed a breathing tube or a pacemaker, and none died. These were only people ill enough to reach these doctors, so the study cannot say how often this happens.
population: People seen in person by medical toxicologists at 50 US sites after loperamide exposure, 2010 or 2011 to 2016 (ToxIC Registry), including people who took it to avoid opioid withdrawal
exposure: Loperamide, in the cases with heart-rhythm problems far above the label amount, sometimes with other substances (7 of 26)
outcome: Heart-rhythm problems (prolonged QTc, wide QRS, ventricular dysrhythmias), depressed consciousness and breathing, treatment needed and survival
magnitude: Prolonged QTc 10 of 26 (38.5%); ventricular dysrhythmias 6 (Results) or 7 (abstract), 5 of 6 after loperamide alone; prolonged QRS 6 (23.1%); myocardial infarction 1 (3.8%); coma or CNS depression 11 (42.3%); respiratory depression 5 of 26 (printed 15.4%; 19.2% by editors' calculation); specific toxicological treatment 17 (65%); intubation 4, pacing 2, resuscitation 1; no deaths. No denominator of people exposed; amount recorded in 9 of 26.

evidence.extracted: 26 registry cases coded as loperamide exposure; intent known for 18: 12 (67%) misuse, 3 (17%) attempted self-harm, 3 (17%) exploratory ingestions by children. Circumstances of misuse, more than one possible per person: taking more than labelled 8, avoiding opioid withdrawal 6, a pleasurable sensation 4. The amount was recorded in 9 cases (amounts only in the card's exposure field).

evidence.extracted: Prolonged QTc in 10 of 26 (38.5%), 5 of whom had ventricular dysrhythmias; 9 of the 10 coded misuse (one aged 17) and 1 self-harm; 5 of the 6 with ventricular dysrhythmias had taken loperamide alone, and all but one of the 6 had prolonged QTc (566-749 ms); everyone with a ventricular dysrhythmia whose amount was recorded had taken far more than the label maximum; prolonged QRS in 6 (23.1%); first-degree AV block in 2; myocardial injury and infarction in 1 (3.8%); no reported deaths.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/_Cross-cutting/Lee_2019_LoperamideMisuseWithdrawal.pdf (online-first version; pages as numbered in that PDF)

evidence.extracted: Coma or CNS depression 11 (42.3%); respiratory depression 5 (printed 15.4%); bradycardia 4 (15.4%); bradypnoea 4; hypotension 3 (11.5%); tachycardia 2 (7.7%); rhabdomyolysis 3 (11.5%); acute kidney injury 3 (11.5%); aspiration pneumonitis 2 (7.7%); seizure 1. By editors' calculation 5 of 26 is 19.2%.

evidence.extracted: 17 (65%) needed specific toxicological treatment, including an opioid antagonist in 6 (23%), sodium bicarbonate in 4 (15%), isoproterenol in 2 (8%) and amiodarone in 1; 4 (15%) were intubated, 3 of them with ventricular dysrhythmias; 2 (8%) had pacemaker intervention, both with ventricular dysrhythmias; 1 needed cardiopulmonary resuscitation, intubation, vasopressors and pacing, and survived.

evidence.extracted: Only patients seen at the bedside by medical toxicologists, so severity is likely overestimated and the cases likely do not represent exposures that were not hospitalised or had few symptoms; voluntary reporting; ECGs not reviewed by the authors and the QT correction method unknown; exposure not confirmed in biological samples in the vast majority of cases.

evidence.extracted: The abstract reports seven ventricular dysrhythmias, five of them single-agent, and describes the 10 prolonged QTc cases as misuse (n = 6) and self-harm (n = 1), unlike the Results.

risk_of_bias.note: Registry of the most severe cases (those reaching a toxicologist), exposure unconfirmed, ECGs not reviewed, and several counts differ between the abstract and the results (card sc_lee_2019, editors' checklist high).

indirectness.note: Worded for cases seen by toxicologists. Read as the risk for anyone who takes loperamide for withdrawal, it would be indirect, as the statement says.

imprecision.note: 26 cases, 6 of them taking loperamide to avoid withdrawal; one or two cases more or less change the percentages.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim from a registry case series starts low (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1 (selected severe cases, unconfirmed exposure, unreviewed ECGs, inconsistent counts) and imprecision -1 give very low. Status single study: the paper cites other case reports and FDA adverse-event data with the same picture (card sc_lee_2019, replication), but none of them was read. The claim gives no amounts: the series cannot show a safe amount, and the amounts are kept to the card's exposure field.
